local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 South Carolina's general election ballot carries county council seats in all 46 counties and, where the term ends this year, the probate judge (36 counties), auditor (26), treasurer (24), sheriff (7), coroner (7), clerk of court (3), register of deeds (2) and county supervisor (3), with 6 of the sixteen circuit solicitors, all on party lines except the council of Fairfield County; and soil and water district commissioners, school board seats reaching 42 counties (on party lines in Horry and Lee counties only) and watershed, fire, public service and public works districts, without parties. Cities and towns set their own election day by ordinance (of 271 municipalities 216 vote in odd-numbered years and 55 in even-numbered years, 29 of those in November), and the Election Commission lists 32 city, town and school district general elections and 9 local special elections as elections of their own on November 3, with 29 more local general elections on other days of 2026. State law sets the election of sheriffs, coroners and clerks of court for presidential years, next in 2028, and solicitors serve four years, so most counties and ten circuits do not elect them this year.
local_calendar.s: S.C. Code sections 7-13-10, 5-15-50, 23-11-10, 17-5-10, 14-17-10, 1-7-310, 14-5-610, 48-9-1220 and 48-11-100 (South Carolina Legislature); the State Election Commission's 2026 Election Calendar and its table of municipal elections; counts from the Commission's candidate lists

local_coverage.t: Loaded from the State Election Commission's Candidate Tracking System as read on September 30, 2026: every county, school and district contest on its list for the November 3 statewide general election, and the 41 city, town and school district elections it lists for the same day: 646 contests and 1,059 candidates, with a local contest in all 46 counties. The list gives each candidate a status, and only those marked Active are shown; 143 others, who lost a primary, withdrew or did not qualify, are left off. It gives no ballot order and never says how many seats a contest fills. It names a school board by its county and a district or seat number, so those contests are filed under the county in the list's own words and the school district is not named unless the list names it. Write-in candidates, local primaries and ballot questions (the Commission lists 2 referendums that day) are not loaded, and a city or town that runs its own election may not be on the Commission's list at all.
